A mismatch is resolved for a key when the list held for that key no longer contains it; if it reappears later, it is warned about again. The message states the configured and the effective value without naming a cause, for example: Group configuration consumer.session.timeout.ms for group g1 has configured value 60000 but effective value 30000 on broker 1.
  • On the share path the same mismatch is therefore warned about once per broker whose leaders report it, and again after the client has discarded its local share session state for that broker and later establishes a new one. The lifetime of the deduplication state equals the lifetime of that local state; the misconfiguration itself may outlive it on the broker.

No client configurations, public Java APIs or metrics are added.

Proposed Changes

Broker

Keeping the configured values. Today the group configuration manager stores only the evaluated configuration of each group, after the stored overrides have been clamped to the broker bounds (KIP-1240). The broker also keeps the stored overrides, so that it can tell when an override is not the value in effect. Describing group configurations is not changed by this KIP.

Resolving the effective values. For every configuration in the table under Public Interfaces, the effective value is resolved through the same code path the broker uses for its behavior: the group override if present, otherwise the broker's own default, after clamping, and after fallbacks such as the default Streams task assignor when the configured one is not available. The diagnostic path does not reimplement any of these rules, and it does not emit the warnings that the regular path logs (for example, the warning for an unavailable task assignor).

Snapshots and tokens. For each group and each response type, the broker builds an immutable snapshot of the entries it reports: Name, Value and ConfiguredValue, rendered as described under Public Interfaces. All entries of one response, the token, and any existing field that carries the same value (such as HeartbeatIntervalMs or AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs) come from the same snapshot. The token is a 64-bit hash of the snapshot's content with entries sorted by name and a canonical encoding that keeps entry and string boundaries unambiguous. A token of -1 is never issued. Brokers using the same hash algorithm and canonical encoding produce the same token for identical snapshot contents, so a client that moves to another coordinator with the same content keeps its list without receiving it again. Different contents may produce the same token due to a hash collision (see Rejected Alternatives). The hash algorithm is an implementation detail; clients only echo the value.

A snapshot changes only when its exposed content changes. The inputs that can change it while the broker runs are the group's overrides and the dynamically reconfigurable broker defaults (the assignment interval and assignor offload configurations). Bounds, other broker defaults and the set of available task assignors only change across a restart. The snapshot can be cached per group and rebuilt when one of these inputs changes; the exact caching is left to the implementation.

Group heartbeats. The group coordinator adds the token and, when needed, the list to successful ConsumerGroupHeartbeat, ShareGroupHeartbeat and StreamsGroupHeartbeat responses at version N or later:

  • The token is always set on such a response.
  • The list is set when the request's token is -1 or differs from the current token, and is null otherwise.
  • Responses with a top-level error, and responses to a member leaving the group, carry no group configuration information: token -1 and a null list. Such a response does not change the client's cache; the client clears its cache as part of its own explicit departure handling (see Client).

Share fetch and acknowledge. The share partition leader handling a ShareFetch or ShareAcknowledge request at version N or later does the same with the share configurations it applies, using its own snapshot for the group. The values describe that broker's local state; different leaders can report different values while their bounds or defaults differ, for example during a rolling change.

Timing. A value describes the configuration as resolved when the broker built the response. The snapshot guarantees two things: that the list, the token and any existing field carrying the same value are consistent with each other, and that they describe the configuration as resolved at that time. It does not guarantee that work already in progress used that snapshot. Session timeout changes are picked up when the coordinator next schedules or refreshes the member's session timer, so the reported value does not describe the remaining lifetime of an already scheduled timer; a new record lock duration applies to locks acquired or renewed afterwards, not to locks already held; an assignment in progress is not recomputed. Changing the handling of the request itself to a snapshot-based model is out of scope.

Cost. The new fields add bytes only to the message body. They exclude the request and response headers, the size prefix and transport framing, and they do not measure runtime cost.

Client

The Java consumer, share consumer and Kafka Streams clients support the new fields. Their behavior does not change: they keep using the existing fields (heartbeat interval, task offset interval, acceptable recovery lag, acquisition lock timeout) as today. The new list is used only for logging.

Cache. A client keeps the token together with the list it identifies, per key: one key for the group heartbeat, and one key per broker for the share fetch and acknowledge path, shared by ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge. It sends the token of the key it is talking to, or -1 if it holds none.

The heartbeat token, list and deduplication state are maintained for the same group within a client instance and are cleared when the client explicitly leaves the group or closes. Coordinator rediscovery and automatic rejoining after fencing or an unknown-member error do not clear this state. Explicit departure includes unsubscribe(), where supported. The client clears the cached state as part of the local departure handling, independently of whether the leave request succeeds. A subsequent subscription and rejoin are treated as a fresh observation for logging. A leave sent because the poll interval expired is not an explicit departure: the state is kept, and the following rejoin is not a fresh observation.

On the share path the client discards the token, list and deduplication state for a broker when it discards its local share session state for that broker: when it closes the session because no partitions remain on that broker, when the broker is no longer in the cluster metadata, or when the client closes. Re-establishing a session after SHARE_SESSION_NOT_FOUND, INVALID_SHARE_SESSION_EPOCH, SHARE_SESSION_LIMIT_REACHED or a connection error keeps the state, and the first request of the new session carries the held token. Partition leadership moving away does not by itself discard the state. A session established after the local state was discarded is treated as a fresh observation.

  • A response with a list replaces the list and the token of that key.
  • A response with a valid token and no list confirms the client's state only if the request carried the token that the client still holds for that key. Otherwise the client resets the token of that key to -1, so that the next request asks for the full list.
  • A response with token -1 leaves the cache unchanged.
  • Losing or clearing the list resets the token to -1.

Logging. The client follows the rules under Client logging in Public Interfaces: the cache and the deduplication state are per key and share the lifetime described above. Configuration names the client does not know are logged in the same way.

Other clients may ignore the new fields; tagged fields they do not understand are skipped, as required by the protocol since KIP-482.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The change is backward compatible in both directions. Nothing is deprecated and no migration is needed.

  • New client, old broker. The negotiated version is below N, so the client sends no token and receives no list. It behaves as today and logs nothing new.
  • Old client, new broker. The request is below N, so the broker does not include the new fields, since they are defined only from version N.
  • New client, new broker. The client receives the list on the first successful response and whenever the reported state changes.
  • Mixed broker versions, for example during a rolling upgrade. Share partition leaders on different versions may or may not include the list. A client only logs what it receives, keyed by broker, and deduplicates logs per broker according to the cache lifetime rules above.
  • Coordinator changes and token generation. A new coordinator with the same content and the same token generation produces the same token, and the client keeps its list without receiving it again. Changes to the token-generation algorithm between releases may cause additional full-list responses, for example on each move between coordinators that generate tokens differently, but do not change client behavior or trigger duplicate logs when the reported contents are unchanged.
  • Non-Java clients. The new fields are tagged, so clients that do not implement this KIP skip them, as required since KIP-482.
  • Release coordination. KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in Apache Kafka 4.5. If this KIP is implemented in the same release, the fields are added to those versions in coordination with KAFKA-20925; otherwise this KIP adds the next version of the five RPCs.

No configuration changes. Clients that do not want the new log lines can adjust the log level of the logger concerned, as for any other log message.

Test Plan

Unit tests:

  • Resolution. For each configuration, the reported Value equals the value the broker uses for its behavior: with and without a group override, with a clamped override in each direction, with a dynamically clamped broker default, and with an unavailable Streams task assignor.
  • ConfiguredValue. It is set for a clamped override and for the assignor fallback, and null otherwise, including for an override equal in value but different in text (for example "060000"), and for a clamped broker default.
  • Rendering. Integers, booleans, strings, lists in configured order, empty strings and empty lists are rendered as specified.
  • Snapshot and token. All entries, the token and the existing fields in one response come from the same state. The distinct snapshots used in the tests produce distinct tokens, the same content produces the same token on different brokers, and -1 is never issued.
  • Heartbeat responses. The token is set on successful responses at version N. The list is set for token -1 or a different token, and null for the current token. Responses with an error and responses to a leaving member carry token -1 and a null list. Requests below version N get neither field.
  • Share responses. ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge carry the leader's own state, and two leaders with different bounds report different values.
  • Client cache. A list replaces the cache. A null list is accepted only when the request carried the currently held token, and otherwise resets the token. Token -1 leaves the cache unchanged. Share keys are kept per broker.
  • Client logging.
    • INFO is logged once per content per key and again after the content changed and changed back.
    • A list received with a new token but unchanged content logs nothing.
    • The same mismatch reported by two share partition leaders is warned about once per broker.
    • A different effective value for the same configuration is warned about separately.
    • A mismatch that is resolved for a key and reappears is warned about again.
    • A leave response logs nothing and changes nothing.
  • Cache lifetime and failover.
    • Coordinator change with the same content and the same token generation: the client sends its token and receives no list.
    • Coordinator change with the same content but a different token: the client receives the full list, replaces the token, and logs nothing.
    • After UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID or FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH, automatic rejoining retains the cached state. Unchanged contents produce no duplicate logs; changed contents update the cache and are logged according to the per-key rules.
    • Explicit leave, including unsubscribe() and a leave whose request fails, clears the heartbeat state; a subsequent rejoin logs the list again and warns again about a remaining mismatch.
    • A leave caused by an expired poll interval keeps the heartbeat state; the automatic rejoin logs nothing when the contents are unchanged.
    • Re-establishing a share session with the same broker after SHARE_SESSION_NOT_FOUND or a connection error keeps the state; the first request of the new session carries the held token and logs nothing when the contents are unchanged.

The new leader is a fresh observation only if the client does not already retain state for that broker; otherwise its existing cache and deduplication state are reused and nothing is logged for unchanged contents.

Rejected Alternatives

An error or status code when a value is clamped. The ticket originally proposed returning an error code. A top-level error code other than NONE means that the request failed, and only the Streams heartbeat has a status list. A non-fatal status could be designed, but it would carry less information than ConfiguredValue: which configuration differs, and both values. A new code value in an existing field would also change the meaning of that field for older clients.

Only the configurations that can be clamped. An earlier version of this proposal covered the 15 configurations that can be clamped to broker bounds. The Motivation describes two problems: clients cannot see effective values, and cannot see when an override is not in effect. The first one applies to every group configuration, and the ticket asks for all of them. The generic list and the conditional sending remove most of the per-configuration and repeated costs that motivated the narrower scope.

Reporting share configurations in the share group heartbeat. The share configurations that govern record delivery (record lock duration, delivery count limit, maximum record locks, renew acknowledge, auto offset reset, isolation level and the dead letter queue settings) are applied by the partition leaders, not by the group coordinator. Each broker evaluates them against its own bounds and defaults. A value reported by the coordinator could therefore differ from the value a leader applies, so each value is reported by the broker that applies it.

A typed field per configuration. Typed fields would be checked by the schema and more compact on the wire, but every configuration would need its own fields and its own logging code, and every configuration added later would need a protocol change. The new information is used only for diagnostics, while the existing typed fields keep driving client behavior. A list with one entry structure lets the client handle all configurations the same way.

Tagged fields on the existing versions, without a new version. This is possible, and there are precedents (ApiVersionsResponse v3, FetchResponse v12). With a new version, the broker includes the fields only for requests at a version that defines them, and a client can tell an old broker from one that has nothing to report. Without it, both would need extra rules. For the request header, the discussion of KIP-1313 also moved from a tagged field alone to a new version with a tagged field.

Sending the full list in every response. This is the simplest option, but names and values would be repeated in every response. ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses can be far more frequent than heartbeats.

The broker tracking what it sent to each member. A lost response would leave the broker believing that the client has the list, and a separate recovery rule would be needed.

An epoch instead of a content hash. A counter kept in memory restarts with the broker, so after a restart or a coordinator change it can reach the value a client still holds while the content differs. A pair of the broker's registration epoch and a per-group counter avoids this and has no collisions, but needs per-group state on every broker and a larger token. The content hash needs no state. Identical canonical snapshot contents produce the same token; different contents may produce the same token due to a hash collision. A collision can suppress an update until a subsequent snapshot produces a different token, or until the client requests a full snapshot with token -1. This is accepted for diagnostic information; a periodic refresh is not added.

Fixing the describe output. Describing a group configuration returns the stored value, not the effective one. That is related but separate: it does not reach the client. KAFKA-20835 addresses another consequence of a stored override outside the current bounds, namely that altering any other configuration of the group fails validation until the stale override is fixed; it does not change what the client sees.

Updating client behavior from the reported values. Out of scope, and it would need its own KIP. The values are reported for logging only.
